skyline.text: Why Amit Varma really did read *Playboy* for the stories
Why Ajay Shah wants every gentle reader to use cash more
The longhand letters to a daughter that became a book

brief.head: The last time
brief.text: Objects leave our lives one by one, unnoticed, Ajay Shah said. He suggests noticing, as it happens, that this may be the last time you do something. {077-C02}

brief.head: Cards, rebooted
brief.text: In the modern world, Ajay Shah said, a visiting card should be a QR code of your contact file’s web address; Google Contacts polls it, so updates arrive automatically. {077-C14}

brief.head: No one-way journeys
brief.text: For most of history, Ajay Shah said, a departure might be forever. Amit Varma read the old Hindu injunction against overseas travel as elders’ fear the young would never return. {077-C08}

brief.head: Zero, the hard digit
brief.text: Rotary dialling meant you knew many numbers by heart, Ajay Shah said. “Good answer, but not the full answer,” Amit Varma replied: zero took the most effort to dial. {077-J16}

brief.head: Only in Calcutta
brief.text: Calcutta’s phones barely worked, Ajay Shah recalled. One woman picked up the receiver, found herself wired into two strangers’ conversation, and heard them talking about her. {077-S12}

thought.text: But we talk too much. You also need a little starvation of connection.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, declining Amit Varma’s idea of a weekly newsletter of long letters

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah unpack a bag of lost objects
lead.head: The things that made us
body: Amit Varma arrived with a massive bag. Ajay Shah, his voice almost gone, wanted to know what it was for. “I have a new voice for you in my bag,” Varma said, then admitted he was kidding.
The bag held objects from his past. The idea, he said, came from a tweet that asked what had gradually disappeared over the last twenty years without anyone really noticing.
Neither host wanted a nostalgia feast. Varma said he was glad to live in this age, and that we have progressed a lot. But some of what was lost, he argued, is valuable for more than nostalgia.

Shah supplied the frame. “We shape our objects and then our objects shape us in ways that go far beyond the simple functionality,” he said. When an object goes, the culture built around it goes too. {077-C01}
## Nothing else to do

Varma’s starting point was the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand’s granddaughter, whose childhood memories, in an episode they recorded, sounded like a beautifully crafted work of fiction. He asked how she remembered so much.
Her answer, as he tells it: “We had nothing else to do. So we looked at things.” {077-S01}
In the 1970s and 1980s, Varma said, books, music and films were scarce. Time was not. “We had a lot of time,” he said, and he spent much of it daydreaming. {077-C03}
Now, he said, we are “scrolling, scrolling, swiping, swiping”, and looking closely has become an intentional effort. He called it a lament about himself, not a complaint about the young.
## Effort as a gift
Then the bag opened: two mixtapes Varma made at nineteen for the girl he would later marry, recorded in real time on a double deck. What mattered, he said, was the effort and the intention.
Shah agreed. By demanding effort, attention and focus, he said, “we harnessed the CPU seconds of the mind into doing this and that created beauty”.
Handwritten letters worked the same way. “When you write, you’re not only expressing yourself, you are shaping yourself,” Varma said. {077-C05}
Shah drew the lesson for today: email can carry the same care, if we choose to write it that way.
## A bag of worlds
Varma’s tour took in his father’s locked cupboard of 1967 *Playboy* magazines, an empty diary from 1986, his late mother’s handwritten recipes and an MTV visiting card that read “Manic Beast”.
Some objects carried whole social worlds. The household address book, Varma said, held everyone you knew, and reminded you of them each time you opened it.
A trip to the STD booth, perhaps once a week, meant a call had to be worth it. The landline was one phone for the whole house, in a fixed place.
Shah, who brought no objects, brought memories: a hostel with one payphone, a three-metre map of India on the family wall, and a father who started CMIE with an evening of inland letters.
He closed with cash. Its anonymity and universal acceptance, he argued, are things we notice only once they are gone. {077-C13}
Varma had the last word: “Cash is freedom.”

second.label: Founding letters
second.head: Sacked, sealed, sent
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how his father started CMIE with an evening of letters
body: On 13 April 1976, Ajay Shah’s father came home and said he had been sacked. Asked what he would do, he said he would start a new organisation, to be called CMIE. {077-S04}

That evening he wrote a pile of inland letters to friends all over India. Each explained what had happened, described the venture and asked for specific help. “And that’s how CMIE got started,” Shah said.
The lesson he drew was for email. A message can be quick and dirty, or it can be an essay, he said: Gmail keeps drafts, so you can edit for days “and only then you punch send”. {077-C06}

quote.text: CMIE got started with handwritten inland letters sent out to friends all over the country

second.caption: how CMIE began with inland letters

third.head: From animal to beast
body: Amit Varma was never the corporate type, or the networking type. But at MTV, his third job, he was told he needed a visiting card, and asked for his designation.
He was a writer there. “I said writer is too boring,” Varma recalled. So he asked for “Creative Animal”, and got it. {077-S09}

A couple of years later came a promotion, a raise and a title along the lines of senior supervising something. Asked what he wanted on his next card, Varma replied with a question. “So I said, What is a promotion from creative animal? So I got Manic Beast.”

Later, briefly independent, he had cards printed that read “Amit Varma novelist and blogger”. {#novelist} As he never networked, the cards others handed him at conferences went into the rubbish or lay around.
third.caption: his MTV visiting cards

p2.title: Object lessons
p2.deck: From mixtapes to cash, what the objects of the hosts’ past did to the people who used them

sections.label: Mixtapes
sections.head: Love, recorded in real time
sections.caption: mixtapes for the girl he married
body: Amit Varma pulled two cassettes from his bag, a TDK and a Sony. He made them at nineteen for the girl he was wooing, who was seventeen and whom he later married. {#nineteen}

Making a mixtape was painstaking. Music from abroad was hard to find. On a double deck, one tape played while another recorded, in real time, and you worked out how many minutes of songs would fit on a side.

That effort was his first point. Making a tape for someone, Varma said, says both “this is who I am” and “I want you to like this”. He made them for friends too, but with the people he was wooing, he claimed a “hundred percent strike rate”. {077-J02}
## Curating yourself

The second point was about the maker. Choosing what to include forces you to ask what you like, why you like it, and why you want to share it with this person. {077-S02} A Spotify playlist, he said, takes a minute to make, for someone with a million other things to hear.
Ajay Shah, “a wee bit older”, had done all the same things. Effort and focus, he argued, had shaped them in ways many people today don’t quite know. {077-C04}
~ His modern substitute: a careful email about a few songs, with links, telling the story of the music and your life around it.

quote.text: When you sit down and you curate the music you love and you want to share, you are in a sense also curating yourself.

sections.label: Letters by hand
sections.head: Long hand, long thoughts
sections.caption: letters written by hand
body: Amit Varma could not find his old letters, but recalled two kinds: sheets sent off lovingly in envelopes, and the blue inland letters in which his mother wrote to him when he was away.

Neither, he said, was a two-liner. Sit down to write a letter and you feel you must make the effort worth it, so you build a narrative. His friend the novelist Chandrahas Choudhury still sends him emails like that.
## Writing to think

Varma tells his writing students that writing shapes the writer, and cites Joan Didion: “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.” {077-J20} Handwriting is slower and physical, and Ajay Shah added that because it resists editing, more brain power goes into it.

Historians, Varma said, can go through the letters of Nehru and Patel. Of Nehru, whatever the criticisms, he said: “The man wrote in longhand.” {#nehru} He doubted today’s leaders wrote letters, and wondered whether they were lesser people for it.

Shah ranked Nehru’s letters to his daughter, which became *Glimpses of World History*, among the great intellectual creations, alongside J.R.R. Tolkien’s letters to his children, which turned into *The Hobbit*. {077-R03}
~ In Class 8, Shah and his friend Manisha Purohit sat one desk apart and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East. They wrote each other letters anyway. {077-S03}

quote.text: Just you’re living two buildings away. But it’s a delight to write and get those physical pieces of paper

sections.label: The diary
sections.head: Chapter one, and then nothing
sections.caption: the diary he never filled
body: Amit Varma’s father, a government servant, received stacks of official diaries every year. Knowing his son wanted to be a writer, he would hand them over and say, “Beta, likho”: son, write.

In the 1986 diary, at the age of twelve, Varma began a novel called *Tales of Saint Johns*. Part one, chapter one was titled “Tantalising Tantrums”, “which at least alliterates”. {077-J07} He wrote a couple of chapters, in handwriting far neater than today’s, and then pretty much nothing.
“So I think of this as an empty diary,” he said, a lament for all the writing he has not done. {077-S06}
## The privilege of paper

The diary also pointed to something he had taken for granted. Getting good at writing takes volume, enough pages that some can be thrown away. In many families, a child had only the notebooks bought for school. Simply having something to write in, he said, was “a sign of great privilege”. {077-C09}
Scarcity cuts both ways, Varma added. A child whose father buys him his one diary will value every page. But the same scarcity can paralyse, letting perfection become the enemy of production.
~ Ajay Shah answered with a line from William Blake: “In what furnace was thy brain?” {077-J08}

quote.text: So I think of this as an empty diary, which is my lament for all the writing that I haven’t done

sections.label: The address book
sections.head: Everyone you know, in one book
sections.caption: the household address book
body: The address book, Amit Varma recalled, lived in one place, on a particular shelf or in the dining room. It was organised alphabetically and was still chaos, with numbers at the back and front and papers shoved inside.
What it held, he said, was “Dunbar plus”: a physical record of everyone you knew, with their phone numbers. {077-C07}
## A tribe in a book

Dunbar’s number, Varma explained, is the idea that our brains evolved in prehistoric times to remember about 150 people, roughly the size of a tribe. {077-R08} Of those, about five are close friends, and a wider circle goes up to about twenty. {#dunbar}

The book held all of them, plus the grocer, the electrician and the plumber. Every time you picked it up, it reminded you that there were people inside. Today, he said, if we are not intentional about friendships, we lose touch with so many people.
He was not suggesting that anyone clutter a house with address books, only that a more concrete sense of one’s universe might help.
~ Ajay Shah remembered his sister Sadna, who has very high standards of being organised, copying the chaos into a new diary every few years. Within a year or two it was chaos again.

quote.text: This is a physical manifestation of all the people you know in the world with their phone numbers.

sections.label: STD booths
sections.head: One call a week, make it count
sections.caption: the yellow STD booths
body: Before mobile phones, Amit Varma recalled, college students queued at night at yellow STD booths, sometimes three together, to call home. It might be a once-a-week thing, so you felt you had to have some kind of conversation.
The booth could also be a site of posturing. A new boy from UP opened a call to his mother with “Pranam, Mataji”, and everyone at the booths turned to stare. {077-J15}
## Always on, rarely urgent

Ajay Shah called asynchronous messaging “a very different frame of mind compared to either nothing or synchronous”. {077-C10} With the bar at zero, he said, we send “did you take your meds today” messages.
The booths themselves vanished. When mobile roaming arrived, Shah said, more than a million booths and their millions of employees went out of business almost overnight. {#booths}

The gloom about lost jobs is mostly misplaced, he argued, citing Ila Patnaik’s newspaper column on the booths’ demise. “Most of the time in India, job loss is not a problem because there is a creative dynamic market economy and people move on,” he said. {077-C11}
~ At IIT Bombay, Shah’s whole hostel shared one payphone. For incoming calls, the watchman came shouting his room number, “two six two”, until he ran down. {077-S13}

quote.text: the watchman would come shouting two six two and then you would run down and pick up the phone.

sections.label: Cash
sections.head: Small change, big freedom
sections.caption: why cash is freedom
body: Ajay Shah closed the episode with cash. “You don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone,” he said.

He asked listeners to think of two things. One is the universal acceptance infrastructure around cash: you can walk up to any establishment in the world, put up cash, and they will take it. The other is its anonymity. “Cash is glorious,” he said.
## The panopticon

In what Shah called dystopian places like China, the infrastructure for accepting cash has broken down. In a fully electronic world, he said, you are fully traceable, and you know you are in the panopticon.
It was a point Vitalik Buterin had made when the hosts were with him in Madras. There is, Shah said, “something beautiful about being able to use cash”.
Shah’s advice to listeners was to use cash more. It is, he said, a social responsibility. {077-C13}

~ Before cash, Shah had talked about landlines: one shared phone for the house, in a fixed place, that might ring and ring with nobody to pick it up. Rigging up an extension cord, he recalled, made it possible to talk in bed. {#extension}

quote.text: Gentle reader, use cash more. It’s your social responsibility to use cash more.

side.boxText: Amit Varma filled a bag with objects, some kept since childhood, others found when he cleared out his late father’s house. The idea came from a tweet that asked what has gradually disappeared over the last twenty years without anyone really noticing. {#tweet}

contQuote.text: We claim that by demanding effort and attention and focus, we harnessed the CPU seconds of the mind into doing this and that created beauty and it shaped us in ways that many people in today’s world don’t quite know.

p3.title: Stories from the bag
p3.deck: Locked cupboards, urgent calls and a map the size of a wall

stories.start: The origin story for me, that in my house my dad had a study
stories.end: published in in the nineteen eighties, and those were New Yorker and Playboy
stories.caption: his father’s locked almirah
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a locked cupboard and what it held
stories.head: What the almirah hid
body: In Amit Varma’s childhood home, every Godrej steel almirah was left unlocked except one. The almirah in his father’s study was always kept locked.

“Obviously, if you’re a young boy, you want to know,” Varma said. Something he was not supposed to see was something he had to see. He found where the keys were hidden and, one day when his father was out, opened the cupboard.

Among video cassettes, books and other random things were magazines: a bunch of *Playboy* and a bunch of *Mayfair*. Varma brought two of the *Playboy* issues, from May and November 1967, when his father was twenty-five or twenty-six. {#dad26}

He reflected on how little men of that era knew. There was no *Debonair* yet, Bollywood offered skewed notions of romance, and there was no internet. “But how are you figuring out what the hell sex is?” he asked.

Then he turned the old joke about reading *Playboy* for the stories around. “No, the thing is I actually did,” Varma said, because the magazine had a great tradition of publishing the world’s best writers. {077-J04}

A collection of *Playboy* stories he bought around 1998 or 1999 is one of his treasured books. It is where he first read Haruki Murakami, whose *The Second Bakery Attack* came out in *Playboy*, alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov. {077-R06}
~ In the 1980s, he recalled, the two prestigious places to publish a short story were *The New Yorker* and *Playboy*. Ajay Shah added the magazine’s interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
stories.why: Scarcity changes what things are worth. One locked cupboard held enormous value when little else was available, and the pages that carried erotica also carried great fiction and long-form journalism. {077-S05}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah first came across *Playboy* in his IIT hostel wing, where, he said, “it was common property”. {077-J06}

stories.start: There's a charming story my friend Arindra Shinoi told in his episode with me
stories.end: for half an hour he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter
stories.caption: Narendra Shenoy’s half-hour call
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a friend’s story of a long-distance call
stories.head: Thirty minutes of Michael Porter
body: Amit Varma’s friend Narendra Shenoy had an arranged marriage with Sheila. Her twin sister had been paired with a talkative man, a great conversationalist. Narendra, Varma said, was not, and felt a lot of pressure. Sheila once even asked him whether he had something to talk about. {#sheila}
They were in different cities while Narendra studied for an MBA. One day he called Sheila, feeling the unstated pressure to be interesting.
“So for half an hour he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter,” Varma said. {077-S10}
~ Varma told the story in a chapter on STD booths, where a rare call had to be worth the trip. “So this is what boys were like,” he said.
stories.why: When a call was rare, it felt like a performance that had to be filled. Young men often had no idea what to say, Varma suggested, and Narendra filled the silence with business strategy.
stories.postscript: The full story is in Narendra Shenoy’s episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*.

stories.start: so I remembered this uh incident from Uh junior college, right?
stories.end: no idea where she is now, and I'm not gonna take her name
stories.caption: the badminton partner’s urgent call
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a signal he missed for years
stories.head: The call that wasn’t urgent
body: Amit Varma went from a boys’ school to junior college at Fergusson College. He did not know how to talk to girls, he said, and could not pick up signals.

There was a girl he played badminton with. One day she rang the bell at his home, which astonished him, since they had only met at college. She had a friend with her, and said she needed to make an urgent phone call. {#urgent} He let her in. She used the phone, and then she left.
It took Varma years, he said, to work out that this was “some kind of expression of interest”. {077-S11} Why else would anyone walk into a random person’s house to use the phone?
~ He has no idea where she is now, he said, and would not give her name.

quote.text: I have no idea where she is now, and I’m not gonna take her name.

stories.start: Um in my home when we were growing up
stories.end: I'm still searching and gentle readers, if you can guide me
stories.caption: the three-metre map of India
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a map that covered a wall
stories.head: India, three metres square
body: In Ajay Shah’s childhood home, one wall, about three metres by three metres, was covered by a map of India. His father had bought the map that the Survey of India sold as four sheets, improvised a wooden board of the correct size and pasted the sheets together. {#map}
After that, Shah said, it was “standard operating procedure”: whenever a place name or a river came up, the children would scamper up to the map and look. {077-S14} He misses it.
Shah has tried for years to build a wall-sized map of the Himalayas, without success. He believes one German company makes a good six-sheet set, and asked listeners for leads.
~ Amit Varma invoked Borges: “The only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.” {077-J18}
stories.why: A huge paper map on a wall made geography part of family life, something everyone looked at together. Shah argued that paper maps give a strategic sense that Google Maps does not. {077-C12}
stories.postscript: Children today, Shah said, can neither read a paper map nor fold one.
